title: Defining business needs and the services to offer
audience: Owners of service businesses who are deciding which services to offer, what each service must achieve, and whether a new service is worth adding to the menu.
referencesAtStart: No regulator page is cited in this lesson. Sources: the defining-business-needs workbook uploaded for this lesson, reworded; a mobile service business plan uploaded for this lesson, structure only.
learningOutcomes: Write a one-sentence need statement that describes the client problem a service solves.
Write a measurable result for a service, with the test, the conditions and the person who checks it.
Assess a proposed service for competition, client switching, substitutes, cost and risk before adding it to the menu.

instruction.heading: Start with the need, not the equipment
instruction.body: A business needs analysis asks what the client must achieve, and only then what the business will provide. For a service business, this means describing the client's situation before choosing a service. A client may want a property to look good for a sale in six weeks, a surface protected from weather over winter, or an odour left by a pet removed. Each of those needs leads to different work, different products and a different price. Write the need as one sentence that names the client, the situation and the gap between what they have now and what they want. Separate the need from the wish: a client may ask for a particular treatment, but the need may be to remove visible wear before a sale. Then test whether the business can deliver the need at a profit, with the equipment, skills and time it has. A service that is easy to sell but cannot be done well with the available skills is not a good service to add. Keep the need statement on the service menu so the team can see why each service exists.

instruction.heading: Stating what the service must achieve
instruction.body: Each service needs a stated result that the team and the client can check. Write the result in terms of what the client will see or be able to use at the end, not in terms of effort. For example, no visible marks on a floor when viewed in normal daylight from one metre is checkable, while the floor looks great is not. For each result, write the test: the light or instrument used, the distance, the checklist, and who makes the final call. Keep the result separate from the method. The result says what must be true at the end, and the method describes how the team gets there. If you write the method in detail, say why, for example because an insurer, a manufacturer or a licensing rule requires it. Link the result to the condition record taken before work, so that the client and the team agree on what counts as finished. Where a result depends on something the team cannot control, such as the age of a surface or a pre-existing fault, write that limit into the result as well.

instruction.heading: Testing the offer against the market and your own capacity
instruction.body: Before adding a service, test it against four pressures. The first is competition: list the other providers, what they charge and what they include, and how easily a client can compare you with them. The second is the client's switching cost: a client who has used one provider for years may not move unless the new offer is clearly better. The third is substitutes: a do-it-yourself product or a cheaper, lower-skill provider may meet part of the need, and your offer must show what the client gains from paying for yours. The fourth is your own capacity, cost and risk. A new service may need equipment, training, extra time per job, extra insurance cover and a stock of consumables, and the work itself may carry a risk of injury to a person or damage to a client's property. Estimate how many jobs per month the service must win to pay for those costs, and check that figure against the time you actually have. Decide to launch, to trial or to drop the service, and set a date to review the decision.

procedure: Write the client problem as one sentence that names the situation and the gap.
List the services that could address the problem.
For each service, write the result it must achieve and the test used to check it.
List the direct costs, indirect costs and risks for each service, including insurance and training.
Check competitors, client switching costs and the substitutes a client could use instead.
Time a trial job, including set-up, pack-down and travel, and compare the result with your estimate.
Decide to launch, trial or drop each service, and set a review date.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented for teaching: the owner of a small service business wants to add a service that removes visible wear from clients' floors before they sell. The owner has not bought equipment and has no training in the process. The equipment price is not stated here: the learner must obtain a quote.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the service be launched, trialled or dropped, and what must be known first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Write the need: clients who want visible wear removed before a sale. Write the result: no visible wear in normal daylight, checked under a light at a stated distance. Then list the costs: the equipment quote, consumables, training time, extra insurance cover and time per job. Estimate how many jobs per month would pay for these costs, and compare that with the jobs the owner can realistically book. Check the insurance policy wording for this type of work before taking any job. If the numbers work, trial the service on a small package for two months and review. If they do not, drop it or subcontract it, and record the reason.

equipmentAndPpe: Notebook or spreadsheet for the service menu and the need statements.
Enquiry log showing what clients ask for, from calls, messages and bookings.
Own price survey of local competitors, with the date of each observation written down.
Insurance policy wording for each service under review.

commonErrors.error: Starting from equipment already owned and looking for someone to sell to.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the client need first, then choose the equipment that meets it.

commonErrors.error: Writing a result that cannot be measured, such as looks great.
commonErrors.prevention: State the test, the distance, the light and the checklist used to decide the result is met.

commonErrors.error: Adding a service without costing the extra time it takes per job.
commonErrors.prevention: Time a trial job and include set-up, pack-down and travel in the cost.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a new service is covered by the existing insurance policy.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask the insurer in writing whether the new service is covered, and wait for the answer before taking the first job.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant any licence, and completing it does not allow you to carry out licensed work. Check the requirement for each service before you offer it.
Before adding a product to a service, check its safety data sheet and label, and confirm it is suitable for the surfaces and tasks in the service.
Confirm with your insurer, in writing, whether a new service that involves higher-risk work, such as work at height or work on a client's structure, is covered by your policy.

qualityStandard: Every service on the menu has a need statement, a stated result and a test for that result.
Every new service has a costed estimate, an insurance check and a review date.
Every trial job has its time recorded, so the estimate can be checked against what happened.
Every decision to drop a service is recorded with the reason.
documentationEvidence: Service menu with need statements, results and tests for each service.
Decision record for each new service, with the costing, the insurance check and the review date.
summary: Start with the client need, then choose the service that meets it.
Each service needs a stated result and a test, so the team and the client agree on what finished means.
Test each new service for competition, switching, substitutes, cost and risk before you launch it.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you define first when deciding which services to offer?
options: The equipment you want to buy
The client need the service solves
The lowest price you can charge

knowledgeChecks.question: A team writes that the floor must look great after the service. What is the main problem with this result?
options: It cannot be checked, because there is no test, measure or checker
It is too short to be useful and it names no date or owner
It names the wrong client and no one has signed it off yet

knowledgeChecks.question: A competitor offers the same service for less, and a do-it-yourself product meets part of the client's need. What should you do before adding the service?
options: Drop both, because price is the main thing clients compare and the service should be cheaper
Compare the competition and the substitutes, and show what the client gains from your offer
Add the service at once and fix any problem later and tell the clients about it then
